tasks.description: Print the text 'Hello, Python!' to the console.
tasks.hint:
`print()` is Python's built-in output function — it displays whatever you put inside the parentheses.
Wrap your text in quotes (single or double both work): `print('Hello, Python!')`
Common mistake: forgetting the quotes turns text into a variable name, causing a NameError.
tasks.walkthrough:
`print` shows whatever is in the brackets.
The quotes tell Python the bit in the middle is text, so it prints it exactly as written.

tasks.description: Print two separate lines: 'Line one' and 'Line two'. Use two print() calls.
tasks.hint:
Each `print()` call automatically adds a newline at the end, so the next print starts on a new line.
Write one statement directly below the other — no separator needed between them.
Example:
  `print('Line one')`
  `print('Line two')`
tasks.walkthrough:
Every `print` finishes by moving to a new line, so two prints give you two lines.
Nothing special is needed between them. Python runs the lines top to bottom.

tasks.description: Calculate 10 + 5 inside print() and show the result. No strings — just the math.
tasks.hint:
You can pass a math expression directly into `print()` — Python evaluates it first.
`print(10 + 5)` computes 15, then prints 15 (not the string '10 + 5').
Common mistake: `print('10 + 5')` prints the literal text, not the answer.
tasks.walkthrough:
Without quotes, Python works out `10 + 5` first and gets `15`.
Then it prints that result. If you had written `'10 + 5'` in quotes, it would print those characters instead.

tasks.description: Print the result of 7 multiplied by 6.
tasks.hint:
Python uses `*` for multiplication (not `x` like in handwriting).
Put the expression directly inside print: `print(7 * 6)`
Other operators: `+` add, `-` subtract, `/` divide, `**` exponent.
tasks.walkthrough:
The multiplication symbol in Python is `*`, not `x`.
`7 * 6` is worked out as `42` and then printed.

tasks.description: Print the result of 20 divided by 4. Notice what type of number Python gives you.
tasks.hint:
The `/` operator in Python always returns a float, even when the result is a whole number.
So `20 / 4` gives `5.0`, not `5`.
If you need an integer result, use `//` (floor division): `20 // 4` gives `5`.
tasks.walkthrough:
The `/` operator always gives back a float, which is Python's word for a number with a decimal point.
So even though 20 divides neatly by 4, the answer is shown as `5.0`.
If you ever want a whole number, `20 // 4` gives `5`.

tasks.description: Create a variable called `name`, assign it your first name as a string, then print: Hello, {name}!
tasks.hint:
Store your name: `name = 'Alex'` (replace Alex with yours)
f-strings are the cleanest way to embed a variable into text: `print(f'Hello, {name}!')`
The `f` before the quote activates the f-string; `{name}` gets replaced with the variable's value.
tasks.walkthrough:
The first line stores the text `'Alex'` under the name `name`. Use your own name if you like.
The `f` before the quote turns the string into an f-string. Inside it, `{name}` is swapped for the variable's value.
The result is `Hello, Alex!` with the braces and the f gone.

tasks.description: Print the result of (100 - 37) * 2. Use parentheses to control the order of operations.
tasks.hint:
Python follows PEMDAS order — parentheses go first.
So `(100 - 37)` is calculated first giving 63, then `63 * 2` gives 126.
Without parentheses, `100 - 37 * 2` would give 26 (wrong order!).
tasks.walkthrough:
Brackets go first, so `100 - 37` becomes `63`.
Then `63 * 2` gives `126`, which is what gets printed.
Without the inner brackets, Python would do the multiplication first and get `26`.

lesson.intro:
Today is about getting Python to say something back. That's genuinely it.
You'll type a line, run it, and see the result. Everything else in the course
builds on that little loop of write, run, look.

sections.heading: print() puts text on the screen
sections.body:
`print` is a built-in function. You give it something inside the round brackets
and it shows that thing in the output. Text goes inside quotes so Python knows
it's text and not a command.

Single quotes and double quotes both work. Pick one and stay consistent.
sections.code:
print('Hello there')
print("Double quotes work too")
sections.output:
Hello there
Double quotes work too

sections.heading: Python can do maths for you
sections.body:
If you leave the quotes off, Python treats what's inside the brackets as
something to work out. `2 + 3` becomes `5` before it gets printed.

The operators are `+` add, `-` subtract, `*` multiply, `/` divide and
`**` for powers. Brackets control the order, just like in school maths.

sections.heading: Quotes change everything
sections.body:
Compare these two lines. The first prints the answer. The second prints the
characters `2 + 3` exactly as typed, because quotes mean "this is text,
don't work it out".

sections.heading: Variables remember a value
sections.body:
A variable is a name for a value. You create one with `=`. After that you can
use the name anywhere you'd have used the value.

To mix a variable into text, put an `f` before the opening quote and wrap the
name in curly braces. That's called an f-string and you'll use it constantly.

watch_out: Forgetting the quotes around text. `print(Hello)` makes Python look for a variable called Hello, which doesn't exist, so you get a NameError.
Mismatched quotes. If you open with `'` you must close with `'`.
`Print` with a capital P isn't the same as `print`. Python cares about case.
Division with `/` always gives a decimal, so `20 / 4` is `5.0`, not `5`.
